analysis.one_liner: Eliminates wage and benefit protections for workers on federal service contracts.
analysis.headline: A bill to wipe out the Service Contract Act, the law setting pay floors for federal contract service workers, never got a hearing or a vote and died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The Service Contract Act of 1965 requires companies that win federal service contracts — cleaning, food service, security, maintenance, and similar work — to pay their employees locally prevailing wages and benefits set by the Labor Department. This bill would repeal that law entirely, effective immediately, even for contracts already signed. It was referred to the Senate Labor Committee and never went anywhere: no hearing, no vote, nothing.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies holding or bidding on federal service contracts, which could cut pay and benefits for the workers cleaning, feeding, and guarding federal buildings and installations without violating the prevailing-wage rules.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the Service Contract Act of 1965 in full, effective the day of enactment [S2] [S3].
The repeal would apply immediately and would bar enforcement of the law even on service contracts signed before the bill passed [S3].

Supporters' argument, outside the bill text: prevailing-wage mandates raise the price of federal contracts and create compliance paperwork, so repeal would lower contract costs for taxpayers. That trade comes at the direct expense of the workers' pay and benefits [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The low-wage workers on federal service contracts — janitors, cafeteria workers, security guards, groundskeepers — who would lose the only legal floor under their pay and benefits.

drawbacks.text: Repeal removes the prevailing-wage and benefit floor for service workers on federal contracts, directly cutting pay for some of the lowest-paid workers doing the government's work [S2] [S3].
The repeal would take effect instantly, stripping wage protections even on contracts already signed and being performed, with no transition period [S3].

Contractors could win federal work by underbidding on labor costs, shifting the federal workforce in these occupations onto lower non-contractor-market pay without any replacement protections in the bill.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings would flow to contractors and show up as lower federal contract prices, but the cost would fall directly on low-wage workers whose pay floor is the only thing the law guarantees them. Nothing in the bill replaces those protections. For the people doing the work, it is a straightforward loss.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died there when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Hank Brown introduced the bill on July 14, 1993, joined by 10 Republican cosponsors [S1] [S4] [S5].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources on the day of introduction; that is the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor vote ever occurred before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Federal service contract workers kept their wage and benefit protections, and contractors did not get the labor-cost relief they sought. The outcome went against the bill's supporters and in favor of the workers the law covers.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Federal service-contract workers kept wage protections

for.name: Hank Brown
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the Service Contract Act and made introductory remarks on the Senate floor.

for.name: John McCain and 9 other Senate Republicans
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the repeal bill; all 10 cosponsors were Republicans.

for.name: Federal service contracting industry
for.what_they_did: Stood to gain from repeal of the prevailing-wage mandate on their federal contracts; the bill's sole policy purpose was removing their wage obligations.

against.name: Edward M. Kennedy
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee consideration of the bill; it sat without action after its referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all 10 cosponsors were Republicans, with no Democratic support, and the bill never advanced past referral in the Democratic-controlled Senate.

industries.industry: Federal service contractors (janitorial, food service, security, maintenance)
industries.note: Repeal would free them from paying government-set prevailing wages and benefits on federal contracts, letting them cut labor costs. The gain comes directly out of the paychecks of the workers doing the government's work.
These janitors, cafeteria workers, and guards would lose the federal wage-and-benefit floor that applies specifically to their jobs on government contracts.
